These exercises go with the Week 4 lecture. Part A checks your understanding of the
ideas. Parts B and C are problems to work through with pen and paper. Part D asks you to
make the paradoxes happen yourself in R. Part E is about your own project. Part F is an
optional R challenge.

A few ground rules:

- **Draw the DAG first.** Almost every question this week gets easier once you have the
  picture in front of you. Pen and paper is fine. So is [dagitty.net](https://dagitty.net/dags.html).
- **Show your work.** Name every path between X and Y and say whether it is open or
  closed. A correct answer with no paths is worth less than a wrong answer with clear
  reasoning.
- **Write in plain language.** If you can't explain it to a friend who missed the
  lecture, you haven't finished understanding it yet.
- Problems marked ★ are harder. Give them a real try, but don't get stuck on them.

A reminder of the words we use. **Holding Z fixed**, **controlling for Z**, **adjusting
for Z** and **conditioning on Z** all mean the same thing. A path is **open** if
association can flow along it, and **closed** if it can't.

# Part A: Concepts

**A1.** Copy and fill in this table. Use the words *open* and *closed*.

| Structure | Draw it with arrows | Through Z, by default | If you hold Z fixed | Should you control for Z? |
|-----------|---------------------|-----------------------|---------------------|---------------------------|
| Fork      |                     |                       |                     |                           |
| Pipe      |                     |                       |                     |                           |
| Collider  |                     |                       |                     |                           |

Then give one example of each from the lecture, in one line each.

**A2.** In lecture we saw three ways to "hold Z fixed". For each study below, say
*what* is being held fixed and *how* (adding it to a regression, splitting the data into
groups, or selecting the sample).

a. A researcher studies the effect of tuition classes on SEE results. She adds family
   income to her regression.
b. A study of back pain only surveys patients at a hospital in Kathmandu.
c. A report compares rice yields in fields that use fertilizer and fields that don't,
   separately for the Terai and the hills.
d. A study of what makes a good employee only looks at people who passed the job
   interview.

Which one of these is easiest to miss, and why?

**A3.** Holding Z fixed *closes* a fork and also *closes* a pipe. So why is the advice
"control for it" for a fork but "usually don't" for a pipe? Answer in 3–4 sentences.
Use the words *confounder*, *mediator* and *real effect*.

**A4.** In the anti-fungal plant example, the treated plants grew more. But when we
compared plants with the same fungus status, the treatment looked useless.

a. Draw the DAG.
b. What is **post-treatment bias**? Explain it in your own words.
c. Is there *any* question for which holding fungus fixed would be the right choice?

**A5.** *Descendants.*

a. In lecture, we wanted to control for wealth but could only measure **income group**.
   Why did some correlation between phones and births remain after we controlled for
   income group?
b. Wealth and hard work can each get you a prestigious job. A study only looks at
   people who earn a high **salary**. Why does this partly open the collider, even
   though no one selected on the job itself?

**A6.** True or false? Give a one-sentence reason for each.

a. Adding more control variables to a regression always gets you closer to the truth.
b. If two variables are not correlated in the data, neither one can cause the other.
c. If X and Y are unrelated in the whole population, they will also be unrelated in any
   sample you take from it.
d. Simpson's paradox, where a trend reverses when you split the data, is usually
   caused by a fork.
e. You can find out from the data alone whether a variable is a confounder or a
   mediator.

**A7.** The **back-door rule** has four steps. In your own words, explain what a "back
door" is. Then explain which step each of last week's examples follows:

a. We did *not* control for height when estimating the effect of sex on weight.
b. We *did* control for living area when estimating the value of an extra bedroom.

# Part B: Name the structure

**B1.** For each story, find the third variable. Say whether it is a **fork**, a
**pipe** or a **collider**, and draw the DAG. (Some have more than one good answer.
Pick the one you believe and explain why.)

a. In years with a heavy monsoon, Nepal has more landslides *and* bigger rice harvests.
   So landslides "go with" good harvests.
b. A scholarship is given to students with top marks *or* to top athletes. Among
   scholarship students, the best athletes have the lowest marks.
c. Districts with more health posts report more cases of TB.
d. A fertilizer trial in Chitwan measures soil nitrogen at the end of the season.
   Comparing fields with the same soil nitrogen, fertilizer seems to make no
   difference to the harvest.
e. Among trekking agencies that survived the COVID years, the ones with the worst
   websites have the best reviews.
f. Households that receive remittances spend more on their children's schooling, and
   their children get better results. Comparing households that spend the same
   amount on schooling, remittances make no difference.

**B2.** *Spot the confound.* For each claim, draw the DAG, name the structure, and say
what you would (or would not) control for.

a. Students who use ChatGPT more get lower marks.
b. Among patients at a large hospital, people with diabetes are *less* likely to have a
   broken bone.
c. After controlling for monthly income, years of schooling has almost no effect on
   whether a household has enough food.
d. ★ Among published studies of a new medicine, the small studies report much bigger
   effects than the large ones. *Hint: which studies get published?*

**B3.** ★ *The low-birth-weight paradox.* Among babies born with low birth weight,
babies of mothers who smoked die *less* often than babies of mothers who didn't smoke.
Does this mean smoking protects low-weight babies?

a. Draw a DAG with: Smoking, Other problems (for example, a birth defect), Low birth
   weight, and Death.
b. Which variable is the collider? What is the path that holding it fixed opens?
c. Explain in 3–4 plain sentences why smokers' low-weight babies look healthier.

# Part C: Should I control for it?

You can type each DAG below into [dagitty.net](https://dagitty.net/dags.html) to check
your answers. But do each question by hand first.

**C1.** *Remittances and school results.* We want the effect of a household receiving
**remittances** on a child's **school results**. Assume this DAG:

```
dag {
  District -> Wealth
  District -> Results
  Wealth -> Remittances
  Wealth -> Results
  Remittances -> Results
  Remittances -> Tuition
  Tuition -> Results
  Remittances -> Boarding
  Results -> Boarding
}
```

*Wealth* is the household's wealth before anyone went abroad. *Tuition* is money spent
on tuition classes. *Boarding* means the child moved to a boarding school in Kathmandu,
which needs money *and* good results.

a. List every path between Remittances and Results. There are five.
b. For each path: is it a causal path or a back door? Is it open or closed right now?
   Name each fork, pipe and collider along the way.
c. For each of District, Wealth, Tuition and Boarding, say whether you should control
   for it to get the **total effect** of remittances. Give a reason for each.
d. What is the smallest set of variables that closes every back door?
e. A classmate controls for Wealth **and** Boarding. What goes wrong?
f. What would you control for if you wanted only the **direct** effect, not the part
   that works through tuition?

**C2.** ★ *A collider that comes first.* We want the effect of taking **Lok Sewa
coaching classes** on **passing** the Lok Sewa exam. Assume this DAG. Motivation is not
measured.

```
dag {
  Wealth -> Coaching
  Wealth -> Kathmandu
  Motivation -> Kathmandu
  Motivation -> Passed
  Coaching -> Passed
}
```

*Kathmandu* means the person lives in Kathmandu. Richer people and more motivated
people are both more likely to move there.

a. List both paths between Coaching and Passed. Which one is open?
b. A colleague says: "Where someone lives was decided *before* they took coaching, so it
   is safe to control for it." Is she right? What happens if you control for Kathmandu
   alone?
c. Suppose you have already controlled for Kathmandu, and your supervisor insists it
   stays in the model. What *else* could you control for to fix the problem?
d. Which rule of the back-door rule does this question illustrate?

**C3.** *A paradox inside a paradox.* Go back to the Berkeley admissions example, with
**ability** added:

```
dag {
  Sex -> Department
  Department -> Admitted
  Sex -> Admitted
  Ability -> Department
  Ability -> Admitted
}
```

a. If we want the **total** effect of sex on admission, what should we control for?
b. We want the **direct** effect (do committees treat women differently?), so we hold
   department fixed. Write down the path this opens. Which part of it is the collider?
c. Why can't we fix this by controlling for something else, if ability is not
   measured?
d. Suppose we *could* measure ability. What would we control for to get the direct
   effect?

# Part D: Make the paradoxes yourself

In this part you build the made-up worlds from lecture in R. Because you make the world,
you **know** the true answer, so you can see exactly when a method goes wrong. Use
`cor()` and `lm()` for quick answers. Copy the code exactly, including `set.seed()`, so
your numbers match your classmates'.

**D1.** *The fork: marriage and happiness.* In this world, urban people marry later and
are happier, but age at marriage has **no** effect on happiness.

```r
set.seed(116)
n <- 500
urban <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
age <- 25 + 3 * rnorm(n, 2 * urban - 1)
happiness <- 5 + 1.5 * rnorm(n, 2 * urban - 1)
```

a. Find the correlation between age and happiness for everyone.
b. Find the correlation separately for urban and for rural people.
c. Fit `lm(happiness ~ age)` and `lm(happiness ~ age + urban)`. What is the
   coefficient on age in each? Which one matches the truth?
d. In one sentence: which path did adding `urban` close?

**D2.** *The pipe: the anti-fungal treatment.* In this world, the treatment lowers the
chance of fungus, and fungus slows growth. The treatment does nothing else.

```r
set.seed(71)
n <- 400
treated <- rep(c(0, 1), each = n / 2)
fungus <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(treated == 1, 0.1, 0.5))
growth <- rnorm(n, 5 - 3 * fungus, 1)
```

a. Compare the average growth of treated and untreated plants.
b. Fit `lm(growth ~ treated)` and `lm(growth ~ treated + fungus)`. What is the
   coefficient on `treated` in each?
c. Which model would you show a farmer who asks "should I buy this treatment?" Why?

**D3.** *The collider: grant proposals.* Newsworthiness and trustworthiness are
unrelated. Reviewers fund proposals with the highest *combined* score.

```r
set.seed(1914)
n <- 200
newsworthy <- rnorm(n)
trustworthy <- rnorm(n)
score <- newsworthy + trustworthy
funded <- score >= quantile(score, 0.9)   # top 10% get funded
```

a. Find the correlation between newsworthiness and trustworthiness for all 200
   proposals, and for the funded ones only.
b. Using the same data, change the cutoff so the top 50% get funded. What is the
   correlation among funded proposals now? What happens as funding gets more selective?
c. Now fund the top 10% on newsworthiness **alone**. What is the correlation among
   funded proposals? Why is it so different from (a)?
d. Selecting the sample is one way to hold Z fixed. Adding Z to a regression is another.
   Fit `lm(trustworthy ~ newsworthy + funded)` on all 200 proposals. What is the
   coefficient on `newsworthy`? What does this tell you about putting a collider in a
   regression?

# Part F: R challenge (optional)

**F1.** *A proxy for a confounder.* Simulate a world where wealth causes both phones and
births, and phones have **no** effect on births. Then try controlling for wealth itself,
for a good proxy, and for a poor proxy.

```r
set.seed(42)
n <- 1000
wealth <- rnorm(n)
phones <- wealth + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
births <- -wealth + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
proxy_good <- wealth + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
proxy_bad <- wealth + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
```

Report the coefficient on `phones` in four models: no control, `+ wealth`,
`+ proxy_good`, `+ proxy_bad`. Explain the pattern using the word *descendant*.

**F2.** *Berkson's paradox.* Two diseases each affect 10% of people and are completely
unrelated. Either one makes hospital admission much more likely.

```r
set.seed(2020)
n <- 10000
d1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.1)
d2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.1)
hospital <- rbinom(n, 1, pmin(1, 0.02 + 0.5 * d1 + 0.5 * d2)) == 1
```

a. Find the correlation between `d1` and `d2` for everyone and for hospital patients
   only.
b. Among hospital patients, what share of people *with* disease 1 also have disease 2?
   What share of people *without* disease 1 have disease 2?
c. Explain why a doctor who only sees hospital patients might wrongly think disease 1
   protects against disease 2.

**F3.** ★ Simulate the Lok Sewa world from C2 and check your answers. Here the true
effect of coaching on the exam score is **0.3**.

```r
set.seed(5)
n <- 10000
wealth <- rnorm(n)
motivation <- rnorm(n)
kathmandu <- wealth + motivation + rnorm(n) > 0
coaching <- wealth + rnorm(n)
score <- 0.3 * coaching + motivation + rnorm(n)
```

Compare the coefficient on `coaching` with no controls, with `kathmandu`, and with
`kathmandu + wealth`. Which models get close to 0.3? Does this match your answer to C2?

**F4.** ★ Install the `dagitty` R package and use `adjustmentSets()` to check your
answers to C1, C2 and C3, and your own project DAG.

# Part G: Reflection

**G1.** Find a news story or a published study that says something like "after
controlling for…" or "among people who…". In a short paragraph:

- What did they control for, or select on?
- Draw the DAG you think they had in mind. Is the variable a fork, a pipe or a
